Solstice Ridge 2P tent review

July 2026 · 11 min read

The Solstice Ridge 2P cost $279 and weighs 2 pounds 12 ounces with the fly and stakes. I bought it in May after a soggy season with a tent that shall remain unnamed, and I spent nine nights in it before writing this: three in a valley, three on a ridge, and three in weather that the forecast had politely failed to mention. It stayed dry the entire time, which puts it ahead of every cheap tent I have owned and most of the expensive ones I have borrowed.

The layout

This is a semi-freestanding design: two crossing poles, one end that clips to a trekking pole or a tree. Pitched properly, the fly extends low and close to the ground on all four sides, which is the single biggest reason a tent stays dry in wind-driven rain. The vestibule is small — enough for a pack and boots, not enough for a kitchen — but it zips from both sides, which matters more than it sounds.

Rain performance

The high-country squall was the test I did not ask for: forty hours of rain, gusts to thirty miles an hour, and a site that turned out to sit in every standing puddle for a half mile. The floor held. The seams held. The fly never wet through, and the interior never so much as beaded, because there was nothing there to bead. I slept dry, and my gear stayed dry, and I have rarely respected a piece of nylon more.

The trade-offs

Two pounds twelve ounces is heavy for a two-person tent, and the packed size is closer to a watermelon than a bottle. The zipper pulls are tiny in gloves, a fix that costs two dollars of paracord. And the inner tent alone is not free-standing, so if you leave the fly at home you also leave behind the tent's bones — a strange omission at this price.

The verdict

Tents get rated on dry nights and sold on grams. The Solstice Ridge is the opposite: a tent that earns its weight when it matters. For car camping, basecamp, and short backpacks where a pound is not the whole story, it is worth the extra money.
